meta.title: Who really said "Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Covey's 7 Habits (1989, p. 101) prints this line — but credits it to Drucker and Bennis. Neither wrote it; the nearest real wording is Bennis & Nanus, 1985.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Covey original: he printed it in quotation marks and credited Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis. Quote Investigator traces the idea back to 1869.

answer.label: No documented author — nearest published wording is Bennis & Nanus (1985)
answer.authorDates: 1925–2014 · American organizational theorist & pioneer of leadership studies
answer.sourceLine: The exact popular sentence is documented in Covey’s book, not in anyone else’s: Quote Investigator ↗ locates it on page 101 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (Simon & Schuster, 1989) — where Covey prints it in quotation marks and introduces it as “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis.” So Covey never claimed it, and neither man is documented writing that sentence. The nearest genuine wording is Bennis and Burt Nanus in Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge (1985), which Wikiquote ↗ cites at page 21: “Managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing.”

source.excerpt: In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, “Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.”
trail: Specialist anchor. Quote Investigator’s chronology of the saying ↗ is the authoritative treatment. It documents this exact sentence at page 101 of Covey’s The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (Simon & Schuster, 1989), records that Covey introduced it as “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis,” and nowhere credits Covey with coining it.

Filed as misattributed. Wikiquote’s Stephen Covey page ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section, noting it was attributed to Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis as quoted by Covey in The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989). Wikiquote’s Drucker page ↗ carries no version of the sentence in any section.

The wording Bennis actually published. Wikiquote’s Warren Bennis page ↗ gives “Managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing,” cited to Bennis and Nanus, Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge (Harper and Row, 1985), p. 21 — published before Covey’s book, and not in the popular form.

The book dates. The Internet Archive’s scan of 7 Habits ↗ confirms a 1989 Simon and Schuster printing. Open Library’s Leaders work record ↗ gives a first publication year of 1985 and lists Harper & Row among its publishers; note that the Internet Archive copy of Leaders ↗ is the 1997 HarperBusiness second edition, so page 21 of the 1985 first edition rests on Wikiquote’s citation rather than on a scan we could open.
source.excerptNote: The attributive frame is the whole story, and it is the first thing dropped when the line is quoted. Strip “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis” and a citation silently becomes an attribution — which is how a sentence its own author gave away came to be pinned back on him. Wikiquote’s Covey page ↗ cites the same page 101 for a sentence that is Covey’s: “Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall.”

source.rightsNote: Both candidate sources are modern books, so nothing here is public domain in the United States: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People was first published in 1989 and Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge in 1985, each far later than the 1931 threshold, and both remain in copyright. The sentence is short enough to quote with attribution, but the surrounding text is not free to reproduce — which is why the Internet Archive scan ↗ is lending-restricted rather than open.

author.name: Warren Bennis
author.heading: About Warren Bennis
author.metaLine: 1925–2014 · American organizational theorist & pioneer of leadership studies
author.bio: Warren Bennis (1925–2014) was an American organizational theorist described by Wikipedia as a pioneer of the contemporary field of leadership studies — a subject that barely existed when he began writing about it. He was provost at SUNY-Buffalo and president of the University of Cincinnati before becoming University Professor and Distinguished Professor of Business Administration at the University of Southern California, where he was founding chairman of its Leadership Institute. His 1985 book with Burt Nanus, Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge, drew the managers-versus-leaders distinction that Covey later compressed into the sentence the internet now misfiles.

copyAttribution: "Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things." — not a Stephen Covey original. The sentence is printed on page 101 of Covey's The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (Simon and Schuster, 1989), but Covey set it in quotation marks and introduced it as "In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis." Neither man is documented writing that sentence: Drucker's version contrasts efficiency with effectiveness, and the nearest genuine wording is Warren Bennis and Burt Nanus, Leaders (Harper & Row, 1985), p. 21 — "Managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing." misattribution.heading: Three men, one sentence, no author
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-quoted sentences in management writing, and it is credited confidently to at least three different people — including one who explicitly said it was not his.

items.why: The sentence really is in his book: Quote Investigator ↗ places it at page 101 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989). But Covey set it in quotation marks and introduced it as “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis” — a citation, not a claim. That is why Wikiquote’s Covey page ↗ files it under Misattributed.

Drucker’s documented contrast is efficiency against effectiveness, not management against leadership. Quote Investigator ↗ quotes him in Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, which it dates to 1974: “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.” QI credits Drucker with those efficiency-versus-effectiveness versions — a 1963 article, a 1965 speech and the 1974 book — and no further.

Wikiquote ↗ cites Bennis and Nanus, Leaders (1985), p. 21: “Managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing.” Quote Investigator ↗ credits Bennis with the leading-versus-managing versions, quoting “leading means doing the right things, and managing means doing things right” from Managing People Is Like Herding Cats (Executive Excellence Publishing, 1997), p. 159. Neither wording is the crisp one-liner.

The earliest citation in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is the Harrisburg Telegraph of 28 August 1869: “There is a difference between doing a thing right, and doing the right thing.” The distinction predates management theory entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody wrote the famous one-liner as their own. Drucker supplied the efficiency-versus-effectiveness distinction, Bennis and Nanus recast it as managers versus leaders, and Covey compressed both into the sentence everyone now quotes — while handing the credit to them. Quote Investigator ↗ lays out the whole chain, and it starts in 1869.

context.heading: How a footnote became a founding text
lead: Covey’s The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People became one of the best-selling business books ever written, and page 101 is where it draws its central distinction: managing is climbing the ladder efficiently, leading is checking which wall the ladder leans against. To make the point land, Covey reached for a sentence he believed belonged to Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis and set it in quotation marks. It is the neatest formulation of the idea anywhere in print — which is exactly why it escaped the page.

What escaped, though, was the sentence without its frame. Quoted on slides, in training decks and in a million social posts, “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis” fell away, and the line came to be signed by whichever of the three names the quoter happened to know. The irony is tidy: a sentence about doing the right thing is now almost always cited the wrong way.
detailsBody: The chronology, as Quote Investigator documents it. 1869 — the Harrisburg Telegraph: “There is a difference between doing a thing right, and doing the right thing.” 1934 — the columnist Elsie Robinson in The Shreveport Times of 18 April, rebutting that idea rather than asserting it: “You think efficiency means doing things right. No; you are wrong! … It means knowing what is the right thing to do.” 1963 — Drucker in the Harvard Business Review: “It is fundamentally the confusion between effectiveness and efficiency that stands between doing the right things and doing things right.” 1974 — Drucker’s book, tightened to “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.”

Then the shift from efficiency to leadership. In 1985 Bennis and Nanus recast the pair as people rather than processes — managers do things right, leaders do the right thing (Leaders, p. 21, per Wikiquote; QI’s own 1985 citation is Naisbitt and Aburdene’s Re-Inventing the Corporation, pp. 20–21, quoting Bennis). In 1989 Covey compressed that into the abstract nouns everyone now quotes. In 1997 Bennis himself published a version closer to the popular form: “leading means doing the right things, and managing means doing things right.” The sentence got shorter at every step, and the author got harder to name.
context.pull: The most-quoted sentence in leadership training is a paraphrase wearing quotation marks.

schema.verdictNote: Two wordings, one page. The text asserted here is the nearest genuine published wording, from Warren Bennis and Burt Nanus, Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge (Harper and Row, 1985), p. 21, per Wikiquote. The popular sentence carried as alternateName — “Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things” — has no documented author: it appears only in Stephen Covey, The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 101, where Covey presents it as the words of Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, and neither man is documented writing it.
